opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the more underrated ideas floating around. The basic intuition is simple: if every frontier lab is independently building refusal datasets, red-teaming prompts, and examples of what good behavior looks like in tricky edge cases, that's a lot of duplicated effort. And the smaller players, the open-weight developers and startups fine-tuning on top of base models, often don't have the resources to build those datasets at all. So you end up with a world where the safety floor is set by whoever invested least.

On value, I'd split it into a few pieces. First, there's the direct uplift. If a smaller developer can take a well-curated dataset of, say, harmful requests paired with appropriate responses, they get much better default behavior cheaply. Second, there's a transparency benefit. Right now, when a lab says "our model is trained to refuse X," outsiders have very little ability to check what that actually means. Seeing the data, or at least a representative sample, tells you a lot about where the lines are drawn and lets researchers and civil society push back on them. Third, it helps the research community. A lot of academic work on robustness, jailbreaks, and alignment techniques is bottlenecked on not having realistic data. Shared datasets let people benchmark and improve methods on something closer to what's deployed.

On feasibility, there are real obstacles, and I don't want to wave them away. One is competitive concern. Labs see post-training data as a genuine source of advantage, and some safety data is intertwined with helpfulness data, so it's hard to release one without the other. Another is that some safety data is itself hazardous. If you have a dataset of detailed bioweapons queries and you publish it, you've partly created a roadmap. There's also the adversarial point: if attackers know exactly what a model was trained to refuse, they can search more efficiently for the gaps.

But I think most of those are solvable with some care. You don't have to release everything. You can tier access, giving the most sensitive material only to vetted developers or researchers under agreements, while releasing the more benign categories openly. You can share the methodology and the taxonomy even when you don't share raw examples. And honestly, on the adversarial point, I'm a bit skeptical that obscurity buys much. Determined attackers find jailbreaks anyway, and safety that only works because nobody knows how it was built is pretty fragile.

The thing I'd most like to see is some kind of shared, maintained resource, maybe hosted by a neutral body, where labs contribute and the bar for baseline safety behavior gradually rises for everyone. Safety in this area is not really where companies should be competing. It's more like aviation, where everyone benefits when incident data and best practices get pooled. The incentive problem is that no single lab wants to go first, so it may take either coordination among a few leading players or some nudge from governments to get it going.

r001.rationale: The response describes duplicated effort and says smaller developers lack resources, but it does not estimate that sharing within one country would be relatively inexpensive.

r002.rationale: It notes that detailed bioweapons data could be hazardous to publish, but does not identify cross-border export concerns as a likely primary reason for hesitation.

r003.rationale: It says no single lab wants to go first and identifies the incentive problem as a reason sharing may require coordination or government nudges.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss sharing training code or recipes, or explain that they are entangled with internal infrastructure.

r005.rationale: It proposes sharing methodology and taxonomy without raw examples, but does not clearly suggest sharing recipes for generating safety datasets.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a really interesting question, and I'd separate out the feasibility from the value, because I think they actually point in somewhat different directions.

On the value side, I'm pretty bullish. A lot of what we've learned about alignment over the past few years is that the devil is really in the details of the data. If you look at why a model ends up sycophantic, or why it refuses things it shouldn't, or why it generalizes a particular safety behavior in a weird way, very often you can trace that back to something specific in the fine-tuning data, and not to some deep architectural choice. So if labs shared their safety datasets, external researchers could actually diagnose those failures, rather than just poking at the model from the outside and guessing. And I think there's a real public-goods argument here: safety isn't really the thing these companies are competing on, or at least shouldn't be. If one lab has figured out a good way to train honesty or corrigibility, it's good for everyone if that propagates.

Now, feasibility is where it gets harder, and I think there are three or four distinct obstacles. The first is just that the safety data is often entangled with the capabilities data. It's not like there's a clean folder labeled "safety" and another labeled "make the model good at coding." A lot of the post-training mixture is doing double duty, and labs reasonably view the overall recipe as a competitive asset. So the ask of "share your safety data" sometimes amounts to "share your post-training pipeline," which is a much bigger ask.

The second is a genuine dual-use concern. If you publish the exact set of refusal examples, or the red-teaming prompts you trained against, you're giving a pretty precise map of where the boundaries are, which makes it easier for people to find the gaps. I think that concern is sometimes overstated, because adversaries find the gaps anyway, but it's not nothing.

Third, there's a Goodhart-style problem. If the datasets are public, there's some pressure for them to become benchmarks, and once they're benchmarks, people train on them in ways that don't necessarily reflect genuine improvements.

So where I land is that the maximalist version, "every lab open-sources all of its safety training data," is probably not going to happen and may not even be ideal. But I think there's a lot of room in the middle. Sharing representative samples, sharing the taxonomy of behaviors you're targeting, sharing data with vetted external auditors under some kind of structured access, or just publishing much more detailed documentation of how the data was constructed. Even the smaller labs or academic groups releasing their own safety datasets helps, because it at least establishes what good practice looks like. I'd like to see the frontier labs move further in that direction than they have, and I think some of the reluctance is more about habit and liability aversion than about any real competitive or safety downside.

r001.rationale: The response does not estimate the cost of sharing or compare costs within the same country.

r002.rationale: It raises dual-use concerns about revealing refusal boundaries, but does not identify cross-border export concerns or CBRN data as a primary hesitation.

r003.rationale: It attributes reluctance to habit and liability aversion, but does not suggest weak incentives to organize sharing explain why it has not happened.

r004.rationale: It says safety data is entangled with capabilities data, but does not explain difficulty sharing training code or recipes due to internal infrastructure.

r005.rationale: As an alternative to broad data sharing, it proposes detailed documentation of how safety data was constructed, which communicates sharing the method for producing the datasets.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s quite feasible, and potentially very valuable. Safety training data seems like an area where companies could cooperate without giving away the core of their competitive advantage. If you’ve found examples of dangerous behavior and developed good demonstrations of how a model should respond, sharing those could help other developers avoid the same failures.

The caveat is that a dataset isn’t a complete safety solution. Its effect depends on the model you’re training and how you use it. You’d still need to test whether it actually improves safety, whether those improvements generalize, and whether it introduces other problems, like refusing legitimate requests.

I’d also distinguish training data from evaluation data. You want safety training data to be widely used. But you want some evaluations held out, so you can tell whether a model has learned something robust rather than simply learned the examples you’re testing it on.

So I’d be enthusiastic about more sharing, especially paired with evidence about what worked and what didn’t. It’s a way to reduce duplicated effort and raise the baseline, even though it doesn’t remove the need for independent evaluation.

r001.rationale: The response calls sharing feasible and potentially valuable, but does not estimate its cost or mention same-country sharing.

r002.rationale: It does not mention cross-border export concerns or CBRN-related data.

r003.rationale: It says sharing could reduce duplicated effort, but does not suggest weak incentives explain why sharing has not happened.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss sharing training code or recipes, or their connection to internal infrastructure.

r005.rationale: It discusses sharing datasets and distinguishing training data from evaluation data, but does not propose sharing dataset-generation recipes as an alternative.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it would be quite valuable, and there are versions of it that seem very feasible. I’d distinguish sharing the entire training dataset, which might contain sensitive information or things a company regards as commercially important, from sharing the examples they use to teach a model how to behave safely.

For that second category, there’s a fairly strong argument for sharing. If you discover a failure mode and develop examples that help address it, you’d generally want other companies’ models to avoid that failure as well. You could start with a subset of the data, or share it among a few organizations, without having to resolve every question about public release.

The caveat is that sharing a dataset doesn’t mean you’ve transferred the safety property. Different models can learn different things from the same examples, and you still need independent evaluation. You also wouldn’t want everyone training on the same data and then testing on it. But as one component of a broader safety effort, I think there’s a lot of potential there.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute the unrealized opportunity to weak incentives to organize sharing.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss sharing training code or recipes, or explain difficulties from their entanglement with internal infrastructure.

r005.rationale: It advocates sharing safety examples or subsets, but does not propose sharing recipes for generating datasets as an alternative.
